Those gaps are listed at the end. Everything below comes from pages I actually read.

---

## Introduction (vv. 21–48)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik, Calvary Chapel):** These "you have heard… but I tell you" sayings are not Jesus against Moses. It is Jesus against false and superficial interpretations of Moses. The scribes made two mistakes. They narrowed God's commands (treating murder as only the outward act), and they stretched them past what He meant (allowing almost any reason for divorce).  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Jesus clears away human traditions to make room for His own spiritual teaching. He changes the rules men made but confirms God's law. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-5-commentary-spurgeon

## v. 25

- **Wesley (Methodist):** The "adversary" is anyone you have wronged in this way. Make it right on the spot, before you part. The risk is that he takes his case to God. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 26

- **Wesley:** "Until you have paid the last penny" really means *forever*, because you never can pay it. He sees vv. 21–26 as being about meekness and what follows as being about purity of heart. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 27

- **Wesley:** Just as with the sixth commandment, the scribes read this one as covering only the outward act. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** He describes the Jewish reading Jesus was correcting. It limited the command to actual adultery by married people and left out fornication and unchaste thoughts, words or actions.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-27.html
- **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian):** The command forbids every kind of uncleanness and the desire for it. The Pharisees limited it to the act, as if God ignored sin kept in the heart.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_005.cfm

## v. 28

- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** The command was about the heart and the eye, not just the outward act. Anyone who looks at a woman to feed lust has already broken it in God's sight.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-27.html
- **Henry:** "A woman" means any woman, not only another man's wife as some argued.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-27.html
- **Spurgeon:** Wandering looks and unchaste desires are the core of adultery, and nobody can claim to have been free of them all their life.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-5-commentary-spurgeon
- **Guzik (quoted on StudyLight):** The act of adultery is still far worse than the thought.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-27.html

## vv. 29–30

- **Wesley:** He reads this as a figure of speech, not a command to literally harm the body. Give up anything, however dear or useful, if you cannot avoid sin while you keep it. The "eye" might even be a person as dear as an eye. He suggests v. 29 points back to lust (vv. 27–28) and v. 30 back to anger (vv. 21–22). So: cut off the right hand if your temper is so violent that nothing else stops you hurting your brother. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 31

- **Wesley:** The scribes and Pharisees let men give a certificate of divorce for any trivial reason. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm
- **Spurgeon:** Moses required a written certificate so that angry tempers had time to cool and any separation was done deliberately and formally.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-5-commentary-spurgeon
- **Enduring Word:** Rabbis disagreed about the grounds. The school of Shammai limited the "indecency" of Deuteronomy 24:1 to sexual misconduct confirmed by witnesses.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Barclay (on StudyLight):** The school of Hillel read "indecency" as broadly as possible.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-32.html

## v. 32: the main point where Protestant writers differ

**The common view.** Divorce is allowed only for sexual immorality. Several writers on the pages I read also say the wronged spouse may remarry:

- **Enduring Word:** An illegitimate divorce leads to adultery because God does not recognise it. A person can have a divorce the state accepts but God does not.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Spurgeon:** Jesus forbids divorce for anything except unfaithfulness to the marriage vow. Adultery in effect breaks the bond, and the state should then formally recognise that.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-5-commentary-spurgeon
- **Matthew Henry:** Jesus took marriage back to how it was first set up ("one flesh"). Divorce is allowed only for adultery, which breaks the marriage covenant.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-32.html
- **Barnes:** No legislature or court has the right to grant divorce for any other cause. People divorced on other grounds who remarry are, by Scripture, living in adultery.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-32.htm
- **One older commentary on the Bible Hub page (the page doesn't name it):** Jewish listeners would hear "put away" as a full ending of the marriage. If the wronged husband could not remarry, he would still be bound to a wife who had broken the core vow of the marriage.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-32.htm
- **Bible.org:** The Greek word (*porneia*) covers any illicit sex, but in marriage it refers to adultery. In that case the innocent spouse may remarry, while the guilty one should seek reconciliation or stay single.  — https://bible.org/seriespage/14-how-protect-our-marriages-matthew-531-32

**Differences in emphasis:**

- **Gill (Baptist):** "Fornication" here is wider than adultery. It includes incest and any unlawful sexual union. A wife divorced on other grounds is still her husband's wife because the bond has not been dissolved.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-32.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** A man who wrongly abandons his wife is guilty of, in effect, handing her over to other men, because the certificate freed her to remarry.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-32.html
- **Wesley:** "Causes her to commit adultery" means *if she marries again*. He comments no further. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm
- **Constable, quoting Hagner:** Jesus brings in the new and shocking idea that even properly divorced people who remarry may be committing adultery. The Old Testament did not see it that way, and divorce should not be an option for disciples.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-32.html

## v. 33

- **Wesley:** Jesus is correcting a scribal teaching that swearing by created things in everyday talk was harmless. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Some argued that only oaths made "to the Lord" had to be kept. Jesus' answer is that every oath, even ones that avoid God's name, is really an appeal to God.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_533-35
- **Henry:** Promises God witnesses must be kept as to Him. Breaking an oath-backed promise is lying to God, not just to people.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_005.cfm

## v. 34: are all oaths banned?

- **Spurgeon (strict reading):** The old law forbade false swearing. Jesus now forbids every kind of swearing and gives his followers plain yes and no instead.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-5-commentary-spurgeon
- **Wesley (narrower reading):** The ban is on swearing by any creature in ordinary conversation. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm
- **Precept Austin (GotQuestions-style answer):** Jesus was not condemning all promises or contracts. He was targeting careless oaths, not wedding vows or legal contracts.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_533-35
- **Barclay (in Enduring Word):** A truly good person would never need an oath. The fact that oaths are still sometimes needed shows the world is not good.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/

## vv. 35–36

- **Wesley:** You cannot change a single hair's colour, which shows that even your head belongs to God, not you. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 37

- **Wesley:** In everyday speech, simply say yes or no.  — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-5.html
- **Precept Austin:** The context is keeping oaths. Oaths are binding even when spoken casually, and God allows no loophole for going back on them.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_533-35

## v. 38

- **Wesley:** "Eye for eye" was a rule for judges dealing with violent assault. It had been twisted into permission for bitter personal revenge. From here to the end of the chapter, Jesus teaches a meekness and love the scribes knew nothing of. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 39

- **Wesley:** The Greek word for "resist" pictures lining up for battle to win. The point is not to pay back evil with evil, and to accept another blow rather than take revenge. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## vv. 40–41

- **Wesley:** When a wrong is purely personal and the damage is small, put up with it rather than prosecute harshly. He says these words are not meant to be followed literally, pointing to how Jesus responded when He was struck (John 18:22–23). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm
- **Henry (v. 40):** Bad people often use lawsuits to do great harm, even when judges are fair.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_005.cfm

## v. 42

- **Wesley:** Give and lend, but only as far as fits your duties to creditors, family and fellow believers, "for God never contradicts himself." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 43

- **Wesley:** God said the first part ("love your neighbour"). The scribes added the second ("hate your enemy"). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 45

- **Wesley:** "That you may be sons" means that you may keep on being, and be seen as, God's children.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-45.html
- **Gill:** The gift of sunshine belongs to God alone, yet He gives it to the most undeserving.  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/matthew/5-45.html

## vv. 46–47

- **Henry:** We cannot expect the reward of Christians if our goodness goes no higher than that of tax collectors.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-45.html
- **Wesley (v. 47):** Jesus may be hinting at the prejudice between rival groups. Wesley wishes the church, split into so many parties, had heeded this and warmly embraced fellow believers of every denomination.  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm

## v. 48: the clearest Protestant disagreement ("perfect")

**Methodist and Wesleyan view:**

- **Wesley:** He reads it as "ye *shall* be perfect." It sums up all the holiness described in the chapter. It is a promise as well as a command, the Gospel promise that God will write His laws on our hearts.  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/5.htm
- **Wesley, *A Plain Account of Christian Perfection*:** He cites this verse. He argues that if love for God fills the whole heart, no sin can be there.  He also insists that this perfection does not mean freedom from ignorance, mistakes, temptation or bodily weakness.  — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/w/wesley/perfection/cache/perfection.pdf
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** The verse answers the question of whether we can be fully saved from sin in this life. As there is no sin in God's infinite nature, none will live in ours.  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/matthew/5-48.html

**Reformed, Baptist and other evangelical views (perfection limited, or a standard that drives us to grace):**

- **Gill:** The perfection is limited to the subject at hand, love for others. It is about *who* we love and *how sincerely*, not loving to the same degree God does, which is impossible. "Perfect" means sincere and upright, echoing Deuteronomy 18:13.  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/matthew/5-48.html
- **Barnes:** Be complete and balanced in your goodness, loving enemies and not just friends. Every Christian may and must be this.  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/matthew/5-48.html
- **Henry:** Either a general call to press toward holiness, or specifically to do good to enemies as God does.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-45.html
- **Precept Austin (critic of Wesley):** It calls Wesley's "Christian perfectionism" an "aberrant teaching" that contradicts 1 John 1:8.  It also offers the reading that God's absolute standard is meant to drive us back to "blessed are the poor in spirit" (v. 3).  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_548_be_perfect
- **Spurgeon (quoted there):** Biblical perfection is reachable, but as balance rather than degree. Grace is complete in all its parts, like a child, yet not yet grown.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_548_be_perfect
- **An older commentary on the Bible Hub verse page (the page doesn't name it):** The word means grown-up rather than childlike, so the call is to maturity in love. It warns against "sects" whose doctrine of perfection either means nothing special or claims what no one reaches in this life.  — https://biblehub.com/matthew/5-48.htm
- **Ellicott:** The idea is reaching the goal or full completeness of our being, which for us involves growth.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-48.htm
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** Jesus is speaking about the *kind* of goodness that marks His disciples, not about how much of it they have.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-48.htm
- **Barclay:** Something is *teleios* ("perfect") when it fulfils the purpose it was made for.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-45.html
